subtype: Approach: telling other classmates his side of the story [Pitfall]
passage:
Monday. Suraj slammed his bag down. "My friend Elizabeth was so unfair about the cricket score," he told the whole class at lunch. "Ask anyone." Two boys nodded.

Wednesday. Suraj heard a new version in the corridor: Elizabeth had cheated and refused to admit it. He had never said that. He felt strangely uneasy, but he kept quiet.

Friday. Elizabeth stood at the classroom door with red eyes. "Why are you telling everyone I cheat?" Suraj tried to explain, but the story had already grown past him, and Elizabeth walked away without waiting.

qa.q: What did Suraj say Elizabeth was unfair about?
qa.a: Suraj said Elizabeth was unfair about the cricket score.

qa.q: What did Suraj feel when he heard the new version in the corridor?
qa.a: Suraj felt uneasy, because the story had grown into something he never said and he no longer controlled it.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Suraj have used, and why?
qa.a: Suraj could have spoken to Elizabeth directly about the cricket score, since talking to the person involved stops the story from spreading. He could also ask a teacher to help settle the score.

qa.q: How does the spreading story feel to Elizabeth?
qa.a: Elizabeth is hurt and angry, shown by the red eyes at the door and the question about cheating, because Elizabeth's name is now attached to something untrue.

grounding: A boy tells the class his side of the fight, the story spreads and grows, and the friend becomes angrier so the fight is harder to mend.
